rule.title: Grounds for Non-Renewal of Lease for Pets in Senior Citizen Housing
rule.requirement: [Basis: official explanatory text, not operative legal text] In a senior citizen housing project, a landlord may refuse to renew a tenant's lease because of a pet only if the pet's existence or behavior violates building, health, or use codes; the tenant fails to properly care for the pet; the tenant fails to control the pet or remove pet waste promptly upon request; or the tenant fails to keep pet waste confined away from common areas and entrances.
rule.exemptions: The Pets in Housing Projects law does not apply to owner-occupied premises that do not have more than three rental dwelling units, or to any health care facility. [N.J.S.A. 2A:42-103 et seq.]

rule.title: Safe Housing Act: Security Deposit Return Deadline
rule.requirement: [Basis: official explanatory text, not operative legal text] When a lease is terminated under the Safe Housing Act, the landlord must make available the return of the tenant's security deposit, plus any interest earned, to the tenant or the tenant's agent within 15 business days after termination.
rule.coverage_conditions: Applies when a tenant terminates the lease agreement prior to expiration pursuant to the Safe Housing Act.
rule.exemptions: The Safe Housing Act does not apply to transient or seasonal rentals. [N.J.S.A. 46:8-9.4 et seq.]

citation.model_span:
Within 30 days after the termination of a tenancy, a landlord must return the security 
deposit, plus interest earned less deductions, to the tenant ( N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.1). Deductions may 
include the cost of any damages over and above normal wear and tear, and any other money due 
the landlord under the terms of the lease. The landlord must return the money either by personal 
delivery, registered, or certified mail. If there are a ny deductions made from the security deposit 
by the landlord, an itemized list of these deductions must also be sent to the tenant by registered 
or certified mail within 30 days from the termination of the tenancy. If the amount of money owed 
to the landlord for damages or unpaid rent is greater than the amount of the security deposit, the 
landlord may sue for the difference. No deductions shall be made from a security deposit of a 
tenant who remains in possession of the rental premises.

rule.title: Prohibition of Source of Lawful Income Discrimination
rule.requirement: [Basis: official explanatory text, not operative legal text] A landlord or rental agency is prohibited from refusing to rent or discriminating in rental housing based on source of lawful income.
rule.exemptions: The Law Against Discrimination in rental housing does not apply to two-family owner-occupied dwellings, rooms in an owner- or resident-occupied single home, and residences planned exclusively for and occupied by one sex, or age-restricted housing as it pertains to familial status. [N.J.S.A. 10:5-5(n)]
rule.quoted_span:
The New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (LAD), 
N.J.S.A. 10:5-12(g) to -(h), prohibits discrimination when selling or renting property and requires 
equal treatment in the sale or rental of housing regardless of race, creed, color, national origin, 
ancestry, sex, marital status, civil union status, domestic partnership status, familial status, 
affectional or sexual orientation, gender  identity or expression, mental and physical disability, 
nationality, or source of lawful income.

rent mid-lease term. The old lease must be terminated, and the new lease must have the increased 
rental payment. The landlord has to offer the tenant a new lease with the increased rent once the 
old lease has been terminated. In order to terminate a lease, the landlord must take the following 
steps (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1(f)): 
1. Landlord must give the tenant proper written notice, which informs the tenant that the current 
lease is terminated, and the tenant can remain in the premises by signing a new lease at an 
increased rent. 
2. Written notice must also state that  end of the current lease, tenant has the right to continue 
renting the premises at the increased rent.

rule.title: Prohibition of Mid-Lease Rent Increases and Lease Termination Procedure
rule.requirement: [Basis: official explanatory text, not operative legal text] A landlord cannot raise rent during an active lease term; the existing lease must be terminated and a new lease offered with the increased rent. To terminate the lease, the landlord must provide proper written notice informing the tenant that the lease is terminated, that the tenant may remain by signing a new lease at the increased rent, and that at the end of the current lease the tenant has the right to continue renting at the increased rent.

citation.model_span:
In some cases, a “Notice to 
Cease” may also be required. A “Notice to Cease” serves as a warning notice; this notice tells the tenant to stop the wrongful conduct. If the 
tenant does not comply with the “Notice to Cease,” a “Notice to Quit” may be served on the 
tenant. There is no statutory time period for a “Notice to Cease,” however, the period of time for 
a resident to comply with the notice must be reasonable under the circumstances (Brunswick 
Street Assocs . v. Gerard, 357 N.J. Super. 598 (2002)).

rule.requirement: [Basis: official explanatory text, not operative legal text] A landlord may evict a tenant for failing to pay a rent increase that is not unconscionable and complies with all laws and rent control ordinances, following service of a Notice to Quit at least one month prior to filing.
rule.exemptions: The Anti-Eviction Law may not apply to two- or three-unit owner-occupied premises with two or fewer rental units. [Exceptions]; The Anti-Eviction Law does not apply to hotel guests, motel guests, or guest houses rented to transient or seasonal tenants, unless the occupant resides there on a continual basis with no alternate residence. [Exceptions]; The Anti-Eviction Law does not apply to a unit held in trust on behalf of an immediate family member who is developmentally disabled and permanently occupies the dwelling unit. [Exceptions]
rule.interaction: The rent increase must comply with all other laws and municipal ordinances, including rent control.
rule.quoted_span:
If a tenant fails to pay rent after being given notice of a rent increase and a Notice to Quit, 
the landlord may file a suit for eviction. The rent increase must not be unconscionable and 
must comply with all other laws or municipal ordinances, including rent control. A Notice

to Quit must be served on the tenant at least one month prior to filing the suit for eviction 
(N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1(f)).

citation.model_span:
Tenants of landlord-occupied two- and three-family dwellings can be removed only when 
a court issues an order for eviction. However, in these cases, the landlord must prove that the tenant 
(a) is staying after the expiration of the term of the lease, (b) is staying after a failure to pay rent, 
(c) is disorderly so as to destroy the peace and quiet of other tena nts, (d) willfully destroys or 
damages the premises, (e) constantly violates the written rules and regulations or (f) violates any 
lease provision where the lease reserves a right of re -entry for such violations. A three (3) month 
notice to quit must be gi ven if an at will tenancy or year -to-year tenancy exists. A one (1) month 
notice to quit is required for a month-to-month tenancy and other types of tenancies are entitled to 
a one (1) month notice to quit.
 
No further notice is required before bringing action in court to evict 
in the case of a tenant staying after a failure to pay  rent. A three-day written Notice to Quit is 
required for any of the causes described as disorderly, destructive or violative of written rules or 
lease provisions (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.2(a)).

rule.requirement: [Basis: official explanatory text, not operative legal text] A landlord who recovers a unit for personal occupancy must personally occupy it for at least six months; if the landlord instead allows another tenant to occupy or registers the property for conversion, the landlord is liable to the former tenant for treble damages plus attorney fees and costs.
rule.coverage_conditions: Applies when a tenant vacates after notice of landlord personal occupancy.
rule.quoted_span:
When a tenant vacates a dwelling unit after having been given notice that the  landlord 
wishes to personally occupy the unit the landlord must occupy the unit for at least six (6) months. 
If instead the landlord permits personal occupancy of the unit by another tenant or registration of 
conversion of the property to a condominium or cooperative, the landlord is liable to the former 
tenant for three (3) times the damages suffered plus attorney fees and costs  (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-
61.6(a)).

scope_inputs.coverage_conditions: Applies when a tenant vacates after notice that the landlord seeks to permanently board up, demolish, or retire the building from residential use.

citation.model_span:
When a tenant vacates a dwelling unit after having been given notice that the landlord seeks 
to permanently board up or demolish the building or to permanently retire it from residential use, 
the landlord must not use this property for residential use for a period of five (5) years. If the 
landlord allows any residential use of the unit during the five (5) year period from the date the unit 
became vacant, the landlord, or the former landlord, may be liable to the tenant for three (3) times 
the damages plus attorney fees and costs. Additionally, the landlord or former landlord may be 
liable for a civil penalty up to $10,000.00 for each violation of this law and the property may not 
be registered as a planned real estate development during the five -year period following the date 
on which any dwelling unit in the property became vacant as a result of an eviction notice stating 
that the property was being permanently removed from residential use (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.6(c)).

citation.model_span:
A landlord cannot take reprisal action against a tenant by eviction, substantial alteration of 
a lease or its terms, or refusal to renew a lease when a tenant exercises certain civil rights (N.J.S.A. 
2A:42-10.10).  The law against reprisal applies to all rental properties used for dwelling purposes, 
including mobile homes, except owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings. These civil rights 
are:  
1. A tenant attempts to enforce any rights under the lease or State or local laws.  
2. A tenant has made a good faith complaint to a governmental authority about a landlord’s 
violation of any health or safety law, regulation, code, or ordinance. A tenant must ha ve first 
notified the landlord in writing and given the landlord a reasonable time to correct the violation 
before making the complaint. 
 
 
 
42 
 
 
 
3. A tenant has been an organizer, or member, of any lawful organization, including a tenant 
organization.  
4. A tenant refuses to comply with changes in the lease or agreement, if the change(s), have been 
made by the owner because the tenant took any of the above actions. If a landlord does take 
reprisal action, the tenant may sue the landlord for damages in a civil action.

citation.model_span:
Foreclosure alone is not grounds for eviction in New Jersey. In Chase Manhattan Bank v. 
Josephson, 135 N.J. 209 (1994) the court held that when a lender or other buyer takes possession 
of the property, the residential tenant comes with the property. Before a tenant can be evicted due 
to foreclosure, the landlord must provide the tenant with a 90 -day notice to qui t when the 
foreclosed property has been purchased by a buyer who wants to personally occupy it as his or her 
primary residence. However, if a tenant has a lease agreement that goes beyond the 90 days the 
landlord may not take action to evict the tenant unt il after the lease expires and the 90 -day notice 
to quit has been given.  The 90-day notice may be given 90 days before the lease expires.  Month-
to-month tenants and two- and three-family owner-occupied units are not exempt from the 90-day 
notice requirements.

scope_inputs.coverage_conditions: Applies to persons acquiring foreclosed properties containing residential rental units.

citation.model_span:
Any person acquiring a foreclosed property containing one or more residential rental units 
must provide notices to the tenants in English and Spanish, within 10 business days after the sale, 
letting tenants know that ownership has changed hands and that the tenants are not required to 
move because of the foreclosure.  In buildings with 10 or fewer dwelling units, the new owner 
must make a good faith effort to obtain the names of all the tenants occupying the property.  
Notices must be addressed to tenants by name, unless the new owner is unable to identify the tenant 
by name, then the owner shall address the notice to “Tenant.”  The notice must also be placed on 
the front door of each tenant’s unit and sent to each tenant via certified and regular mail (N.J.S.A. 
2A:50-69 et seq.). 
 
 
 
43 
 
 
 
 In a residential property containing more than 10 dwelling units, the new owner must 
provide notice to tenants occupying the property by conspicuously displaying a copy of the 
“NOTICE TO TENANTS” in a prominent location, such as a common area of the building or other 
structure on the property.  If there is no common area, the notice must be posted in a conspicuous 
location in each building, such as the walls of the front vestibule or any foyer or hallway near the 
main entrance of the building (N.J.S.A. 2A:50-70(c)2).

citation.model_span:
When making a bona fide monetary offer to induce tena nts to move, the new owner must 
provide a separate and different notice from the notice required to be given by a foreclosing 
creditor.  The new owner must provide a copy of the “NOTICE TO TENANTS” and give it with 
the initial and final written or verbal offer to the tenant.   
 The foreclosing agency, including a bank, creditor, or a new landlord may make a written 
bona fide (good faith) monetary offer requesting that the tenant vacate the property, without “good 
cause.”  An acceptance of the offer by the t enant must be in writing and include an 
acknowledgement of the date of the receipt of the offer, and an understanding that the tenant had 
a five-day review period to accept or reject the offer presented.   
 However, it is important to note that the accepta nce of a bona fide monetary offer is 
voluntary.  The tenant shall not be pressured by anyone, including the person making the offer to 
accept any offer to vacate the property.  Pursuant to the New Jersey Foreclosure Fairness Act 
(N.J.S.A. 2A:50-69 et seq.), pressure tactics include but are not limited to (N.J.S.A. 2A:50-71(b)): 
1. Mischaracterizing or misrepresenting the rights of the tenant under the law; 
2. Implying the tenant is obligated to accept the offer;  
3. Implying that there will be consequences against the tenant for failing to accept the offer; 
4. Harassment, including but not limited to discontinuance of utilities, failure to maintain 
common areas or fa cilities, or any other failure to maintain the premises in a habitable 
condition; and 
5. An increase in rent in excess of any rent control or rent leveling ordinance, or if the property 
is not subject to rent control, an unreasonable or unconscionable rent increase.

rule.title: Foreclosure Monetary Offers to Vacate and Pressure Tactics Ban

citation.model_span:
The Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act protects senior citizens who meet 
certain eligibility requirements (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.22 to -61.39; N.J.A.C. 5:24-2.1 to -2.11). To 
qualify, tenants must :  (1) be at least 62 years of age before the d ate of the conversion recording 
of the condominium or cooperative; or (2) be permanently disabled; or (3)  be  honorably 
discharged from any military service under certain circumstances from any branch of the U.S. 
Armed Forces and disabled at 60% or higher resulting from said service and, (4) live in a building 
being converted to a condominium, cooperative; or fee simple ownership of units at least one (1) 
year prior to the conversion recording date. Tenants may be protected from eviction for 40 years 
if their family income is not more than three (3) times the average per person income in their 
county or $50,000.00, whichever  is greater (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.28).

provisions.summary: Prohibition on entrance fees or start-of-tenancy payments to enter a mobile home park, with double damages remedy.
Requirement of good cause for a residential landlord to refuse to renew a lease.
Circumstances under which a landlord in senior housing may refuse to renew a lease because of a pet.
Eviction action for lease violation if a pet is an unremoved continuing nuisance, with burden of proof on the landlord.
Restricts lease termination and prohibits eviction solely because the lease term has ended.
Landlord must make security deposit and interest available within 15 business days after Safe Housing Act lease termination.
Notice requirements within 3 business days regarding location and hours to pick up security deposit, including duplicate notice to relocation officer or clerk.
Security deposit return availability period of 30 days, itemization requirement, and reinvestment of unclaimed funds.
Permissible deductions from security deposit upon early termination.
Court stay of eviction actions for up to three months for service members meeting rent threshold.
Limits on initial security deposits, annual increases, pet deposits, and advance rents.
Requirement that security deposits be held in trust and not commingled.
Banking and investment account rules for holding security deposits, based on the number of units.
Duty to pay or credit security deposit interest or earnings annually to the tenant.
Notice of banking institution and account details, transfer notice, and tenant remedy to apply deposit to rent for landlord non-compliance.
Duty to return deposit and interest within 30 days of termination, permitted deductions, and itemization notice.
Double damages remedy for wrongful withholding of security deposit, and return timeline in a broken lease.
Duty to return security deposit within five business days when a tenant is displaced by fire, flood, condemnation, or evacuation.
Duty of new owner upon property transfer to handle, invest, give notice, pay interest, and return security deposit.

scope_mappings.target_anchor: A landlord may ref use to renew a tenant’s
scope_mappings.target_quote:
A landlord may ref use to renew a tenant’s lease because of a pet, under the following 
circumstances: 
1. If the pet’s existence or behavior violates federal, state, or local building, health or use 
codes; 
2. If the tenant fails to properly care for the pet; 
3. If the tenant fails to control the pet, when taking the pet to or from the building, or if the 
tenant fails to take prompt action to remove any pet waste when requested by the landlord; 
and 
4. If the tenant fails to keep the pet’s waste functions confined to areas that do not inter fere 
with the common areas or entrance and exist of anyone to or from the senior citizen housing 
project.

decision.reason: The exemption for small owner-occupied premises and health care facilities limits the senior citizen housing project pet non-renewal provisions.

scope_mappings.statement: Account and holding requirements under N.J.S.A. 46:8-19 do not apply to security deposits for seasonal use or rental of not more than 125 consecutive days by a person with a permanent residence elsewhere, excluding living quarters for seasonal, temporary, or migrant farm workers.
scope_mappings.scope_words:
This 
section of the Security Deposit Law does not apply
scope_mappings.condition_evidence:
This 
section of the Security Deposit Law does not apply to security deposits for seasonal use or rental. 
Seasonal use or rental means use or rental for a term of not more than 125 consecutive days for 
residential purposes by a person having a permanent  place of residence elsewhere. Seasonal use 
or rental does not mean use or rental of living quarters for seasonal, temporary, or migrant farm 
workers in connection with work or place where work is being performed. The landlord shall have 
the burden of proving that the use or rental of the residential property is seasonal ( N.J.S.A. 46:8-
19 (d)).
scope_mappings.target_anchor: The security deposit money continues to be the property of
scope_mappings.target_quote:
The security deposit money continues to be the property of the person making the deposit 
and must be held in trust by the person receiving the money. This means that the person who 
receives the money must not use the money in any way not permitted by law. The security deposit 
shall not be comingled with the personal property or become an asset of the landlord.

decision.reason: The seasonal rental exemption under N.J.S.A. 46:8-19(d) expressly limits the trust and anti-commingling duties in that section.

scope_mappings.target_anchor: A. Failure to Pay Rent
scope_mappings.target_quote:
If a tenant fails to pay rent, the landlord may immediately take legal action to have the 
tenant evicted. The landlord is not required to give the tenant notice before filing an 
eviction suit, except if the tenant resides in federally subsidized housing. I f the tenant 
resides in federally subsidized housing a 14-day notice must be given before filing a suite 
for eviction (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1(a)).

decision.reason: The owner-occupied two- or three-unit dwelling exception applies to evictions for nonpayment of rent under the Anti-Eviction Act.

scope_mappings.target_anchor: D. Substantial Violation or Breach of the Landlord’s Rules
scope_mappings.target_quote:
If after given a written Notice to Cease violating or breaching reasonable rules and 
regulations contained in the lease or accepted in writing by the tenant, the tenant continues 
to substantially violate or breach the rules and regulations, the  landlord may file a suit for 
eviction. A Notice to Quit must be served on the tenant at least one month prior to filing 
the suit for eviction. In addition, any notices must be given on or before the start of a 
new month (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1(d)).

decision.reason: The owner-occupied two- or three-unit dwelling exception applies to evictions for rules violations under the Anti-Eviction Act.

scope_mappings.target_quote:
If a tenant resides in the property on the condition that, he is employed by the landlord as 
a superintendent, janitor, or in some other job and that employment is terminated the

days prior to filing a suit for eviction (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1(m)).

decision.reason: The owner-occupied two- or three-unit dwelling exception applies to evictions based on termination of employment.

scope_mappings.target_anchor: A. Failure to Pay Rent
scope_mappings.target_quote:
If a tenant fails to pay rent, the landlord may immediately take legal action to have the 
tenant evicted. The landlord is not required to give the tenant notice before filing an 
eviction suit, except if the tenant resides in federally subsidized housing. I f the tenant 
resides in federally subsidized housing a 14-day notice must be given before filing a suite 
for eviction (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1(a)).

decision.reason: The transient and seasonal tenant exception limits the Anti-Eviction Act's nonpayment of rent eviction provisions.

2A:18-61.1(b)).

decision.reason: The transient and seasonal tenant exception limits the Anti-Eviction Act's disorderly conduct eviction provisions.

scope_mappings.target_anchor: D. Substantial Violation or Breach of the Landlord’s Rules
scope_mappings.target_quote:
If after given a written Notice to Cease violating or breaching reasonable rules and 
regulations contained in the lease or accepted in writing by the tenant, the tenant continues 
to substantially violate or breach the rules and regulations, the  landlord may file a suit for 
eviction. A Notice to Quit must be served on the tenant at least one month prior to filing 
the suit for eviction. In addition, any notices must be given on or before the start of a 
new month (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1(d)).

decision.reason: The transient and seasonal tenant exception limits the Anti-Eviction Act's rules violation eviction provisions.

scope_mappings.target_quote:

may file suit for eviction. A Notice to Quit must be served on the tenant at least 18 months

(N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1(h)).

decision.reason: The transient and seasonal tenant exception limits the Anti-Eviction Act's permanent retirement from residential use eviction provisions.

      "source_basis": "official_explanatory_text",
      "quote_parts": [

          "quoted_text": "When a tenant vacates a dwelling unit after having been given notice that the landlord seeks \nto permanently board up or demolish the building or to permanently retire it from residential use, \nthe landlord must not use this property for residential use for a period of five (5) years.     {
      "category": "just_cause_eviction",
      "citation": "N.J.S.A. 2A:42-10.10",
      "provision_ids": ["P12"],
      "source_basis": "official_explanatory_text",
      "quote_parts": [
        {
          "segment_id": 1,
          "quoted_text": "A landlord cannot take reprisal action against a tenant by eviction, substantial alteration of \na lease or its terms, or refusal to renew a lease when a tenant exercises certain civil rights (N.J.S.A. \n2A:42-10.10).  The law against reprisal applies to all rental properties used for dwelling purposes, \nincluding mobile homes, except owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings. These civil rights \nare:  \n1. A tenant attempts to enforce any rights under the lease or State or local laws.  \n2. A tenant has made a good faith complaint to a governmental authority about a landlord’s \nviolation of any health or safety law, regulation, code, or ordinance. A tenant must ha ve first \nnotified the landlord in writing and given the landlord a reasonable time to correct the violation \nbefore making the complaint. \n \n \n \n42 \n \n \n \n3. A tenant has been an organizer, or member, of any lawful organization, including a tenant \norganization.  \n4. A tenant refuses to comply with changes in the lease or agreement, if the change(s), have been \nmade by the owner because the tenant took any of the above actions. If a landlord does take \nreprisal action, the tenant may sue the landlord for damages in a civil action."
        }
      ],
      "title": "Prohibition Against Retaliatory Eviction and Reprisal",
      "requirement": "A landlord cannot take reprisal action by eviction, lease alteration, or lease non-renewal when a tenant attempts to enforce rights, makes good faith health/safety complaints after written notice and reasonable time to correct, organizes or joins a tenant group, or refuses retaliatory lease changes. A tenant subject to reprisal may sue for damages in a civil action.",

    {
      "category": "just_cause_eviction",
      "citation": "Chase Manhattan Bank v. Josephson, 135 N.J. 209 (1994)",
      "provision_ids": ["P15"],
      "source_basis": "official_explanatory_text",
      "quote_parts": [
        {
          "segment_id": 1,
          "quoted_text": "Foreclosure alone is not grounds for eviction in New Jersey. In Chase Manhattan Bank v. \nJosephson, 135 N.J. 209 (1994) the court held that when a lender or other buyer takes possession \nof the property, the residential tenant comes with the property. Before a tenant can be evicted due \nto foreclosure, the landlord must provide the tenant with a 90 -day notice to qui t when the \nforeclosed property has been purchased by a buyer who wants to personally occupy it as his or her \nprimary residence. However, if a tenant has a lease agreement that goes beyond the 90 days the \nlandlord may not take action to evict the tenant unt il after the lease expires and the 90 -day notice \nto quit has been given.  The 90-day notice may be given 90 days before the lease expires.  Month-\nto-month tenants and two- and three-family owner-occupied units are not exempt from the 90-day \nnotice requirements."
        }
      ],
      "title": "Foreclosure Eviction Restrictions and 90-Day Notice to Quit",
      "requirement": "Foreclosure alone is not grounds for eviction; a buyer seeking to personally occupy the foreclosed property must provide a 90-day notice to quit and cannot evict the tenant until any lease exceeding 90 days expires. Month-to-month tenancies and two- and three-family owner-occupied units are not exempt from the 90-day notice requirement.",

    {
      "category": "just_cause_eviction",
      "citation": "N.J.S.A. 2A:50-69 et seq.",
      "provision_ids": ["P16"],
      "source_basis": "official_explanatory_text",
      "quote_parts": [
        {
          "segment_id": 1,
          "quoted_text": "Any person acquiring a foreclosed property containing one or more residential rental units \nmust provide notices to the tenants in English and Spanish, within 10 business days after the sale, \nletting tenants know that ownership has changed hands and that the tenants are not required to \nmove because of the foreclosure.  In buildings with 10 or fewer dwelling units, the new owner \nmust make a good faith effort to obtain the names of all the tenants occupying the property.  \nNotices must be addressed to tenants by name, unless the new owner is unable to identify the tenant \nby name, then the owner shall address the notice to “Tenant.”  The notice must also be placed on \nthe front door of each tenant’s unit and sent to each tenant via certified and regular mail (N.J.S.A. \n2A:50-69 et seq.). \n \n \n \n43 \n \n \n \n In a residential property containing more than 10 dwelling units, the new owner must \nprovide notice to tenants occupying the property by conspicuously displaying a copy of the \n“NOTICE TO TENANTS” in a prominent location, such as a common area of the building or other \nstructure on the property.  If there is no common area, the notice must be posted in a conspicuous \nlocation in each building, such as the walls of the front vestibule or any foyer or hallway near the \nmain entrance of the building (N.J.S.A. 2A:50-70(c)2)."
        }
      ],

      "requirement": "Any person acquiring a foreclosed property with residential rental units must provide notice in English and Spanish within 10 business days after the sale informing tenants that ownership has transferred and they are not required to move.       "quote_parts": [

          "segment_id": 1,
          "quoted_text": "Any written or verbal communication, including a summons and complaint, an initial \nwritten or verbal communication by a foreclosing creditor, or any communication written or verbal \nthat requests a tenant to vacate the property before the foreclosure or sale of the property, requires \nthe foreclosing creditor to give notice to the tenants as outlined in the  New Jersey Court Rules, \nentitled “Notice to Residential Tenants of Rights During Foreclosure,”  (APPENDIX XII-K)."

    {
      "category": "just_cause_eviction",
      "citation": "N.J.S.A. 2A:50-71(b)",
      "provision_ids": ["P18"],
      "source_basis": "official_explanatory_text",
      "quote_parts": [
        {
          "segment_id": 1,
          "quoted_text": "When making a bona fide monetary offer to induce tena nts to move, the new owner must \nprovide a separate and different notice from the notice required to be given by a foreclosing \ncreditor.  The new owner must provide a copy of the “NOTICE TO TENANTS” and give it with \nthe initial and final written or verbal offer to the tenant.   \n The foreclosing agency, including a bank, creditor, or a new landlord may make a written \nbona fide (good faith) monetary offer requesting that the tenant vacate the property, without “good \ncause.”  An acceptance of the offer by the t enant must be in writing and include an \nacknowledgement of the date of the receipt of the offer, and an understanding that the tenant had \na five-day review period to accept or reject the offer presented.   \n However, it is important to note that the accepta nce of a bona fide monetary offer is \nvoluntary.  The tenant shall not be pressured by anyone, including the person making the offer to \naccept any offer to vacate the property.  Pursuant to the New Jersey Foreclosure Fairness Act \n(N.J.S.A. 2A:50-69 et seq.), pressure tactics include but are not limited to (N.J.S.A. 2A:50-71(b)): \n1. Mischaracterizing or misrepresenting the rights of the tenant under the law; \n2. Implying the tenant is obligated to accept the offer;  \n3. Implying that there will be consequences against the tenant for failing to accept the offer; \n4. Harassment, including but not limited to discontinuance of utilities, failure to maintain \ncommon areas or fa cilities, or any other failure to maintain the premises in a habitable \ncondition; and \n5. An increase in rent in excess of any rent control or rent leveling ordinance, or if the property \nis not subject to rent control, an unreasonable or unconscionable rent increase."
        }
      ],

      "requirement": "Monetary offers to induce tenants to vacate must be in writing, accompanied by the required notice, allow a five-day review period, and remain strictly voluntary. Owners and foreclosing agencies are prohibited from using pressure tactics, including misrepresenting tenant rights, implying acceptance is mandatory, threatening consequences, harassment, habitable condition failures, or rent increases exceeding rent leveling ordinances or unconscionable amounts.",
      "key_value": "5-day review period",

      "quote_parts": [

          "quoted_text": "The Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act protects senior citizens who meet \ncertain eligibility requirements (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.22 to -61.39; N.J.A.C. 5:24-2.1 to -2.11). To \nqualify, tenants must :  (1) be at least 62 years of age before the d ate of the conversion recording \nof the condominium or cooperative; or (2) be permanently disabled; or (3)  be  honorably \ndischarged from any military service under certain circumstances from any branch of the U.S. \nArmed Forces and disabled at 60% or higher resulting from said service and, (4) live in a building \nbeing converted to a condominium, cooperative; or fee simple ownership of units at least one (1) \nyear prior to the conversion recording date. Tenants may be protected from eviction for 40 years \nif their family income is not more than three (3) times the average per person income in their \ncounty or $50,000.00, whichever  is greater (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.28)."

mappings.statement: Account and holding requirements under N.J.S.A. 46:8-19 do not apply to security deposits for seasonal use or rental of not more than 125 consecutive days by a person with a permanent residence elsewhere, excluding living quarters for seasonal, temporary, or migrant farm workers.
mappings.scope_words:
This 
section of the Security Deposit Law does not apply
mappings.condition_evidence:
This 
section of the Security Deposit Law does not apply to security deposits for seasonal use or rental. 
Seasonal use or rental means use or rental for a term of not more than 125 consecutive days for 
residential purposes by a person having a permanent  place of residence elsewhere. Seasonal use 
or rental does not mean use or rental of living quarters for seasonal, temporary, or migrant farm 
workers in connection with work or place where work is being performed. The landlord shall have 
the burden of proving that the use or rental of the residential property is seasonal ( N.J.S.A. 46:8-
19 (d)).
mappings.target_anchor: The security deposit money continues to be the property of
mappings.target_quote:
The security deposit money continues to be the property of the person making the deposit 
and must be held in trust by the person receiving the money. This means that the person who 
receives the money must not use the money in any way not permitted by law. The security deposit 
shall not be comingled with the personal property or become an asset of the landlord.

decision.reason: The seasonal rental exemption under N.J.S.A. 46:8-19(d) expressly limits the trust and anti-commingling duties in that section.
